narrative:
Your application was denied because the model assessed your chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt at nearly 57 percent. In plain terms, that means the model saw you as more likely to fail than to pass—a risk the admissions committee was not willing to take.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by how strongly they influenced the outcome. The most influential by far was your class standing in your third year. You placed in the second decile of your class, meaning you finished in the bottom 20 percent of your peer group. This is a severe contrast to accepted students, who on average sat in the sixth decile. The model weighed this as a strong signal pointing toward bar exam failure—understandably, because students who struggle in the latter years of law school often carry that difficulty into the high-stakes exam.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor, but here the influence worked in your favor. At 3.20, your GPA is essentially on par with the accepted-student average of 3.23. The model treated this as evidence pushing toward passing, a meaningful counterbalance, but not enough to offset the larger concern of your third-year performance.

Finally, your first-year class standing also contributed to the failure prediction. You were again in the second decile, compared to an average of sixth for accepted students. While this mattered less than your third-year standing, it reinforced the overall picture that you have frequently ranked near the bottom of your cohort.

To strengthen a future application, focus first on raising your class rank substantially during the remainder of your studies—perhaps by prioritizing bar-related coursework—since this was the dominant red flag the model identified.
